National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997 (NLSY97)About · Using this site

About this site

This site describes the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997 (NLSY97), published by U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS); produced and distributed by the Center for Human Resource Research (CHRR), The Ohio State University. It is generated from the repository pdt-nlsy97, which holds metadata built from the publisher's documentation: each variable's label, question text, codes and missing codes, and availability, with corrections and links between releases. Each fact says where it came from.

What it isn't

  • It isn't the publisher's site, and the publisher hasn't reviewed it. The publisher's own page for the dataset is https://www.nlsinfo.org/content/cohorts/nlsy97. Where this site and the publisher's documentation differ, the publisher's documentation is the source; the differences this repository knows of are listed as corrections.
  • It doesn't hold the data. The data come from the publisher, or from this repository's data release when the terms allow; see Getting the data.
  • It makes no analysis decisions: which answers count as agreement, which weights or cases to use, or how to recode. Those belong to the projects that use the data.

What they say
What NLS says (read 2026-11-20): public-use data are available at no cost through the NLS Investigator, and whole-cohort files are posted for download (https://www.nlsinfo.org/content/access-data-investigator/accessing-data-cohorts); "It is not necessary to get an account to browse data, but an account is necessary to save datasets online" (https://www.nlsinfo.org/content/getting-started/accessing-data). The suggested citation is at https://www.nlsinfo.org/bibliography/citing-nls-data. The site's System Use Notification limits use of the Investigator to "intended, lawful purposes". No statement about redistributing the public-use files was found. Geocode data are restricted (a separate application) and aren't used here.

Reporting an error

  • In the publisher's documentation (a wrong label, a missing code, question text that belongs to another item): open an issue at https://github.com/AllenDowney/pdt-nlsy97/issues, with where you found it. This repository records such errors as corrections, with the evidence, and keeps the publisher's original; it also says whether the error was reported to the publisher.
  • In this repository's records (a wrong link, a code classified wrongly, a variable left out): open an issue at https://github.com/AllenDowney/pdt-nlsy97/issues.
  • To the publisher: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS); produced and distributed by the Center for Human Resource Research (CHRR), The Ohio State University.

Notes

From the repository's AGENT_NOTES.md, written by hand: what the records can't say.

Answers spread across rounds

Written by Claude (PublicDataToolkit Task 69), 2026-11-20, from NLS's documentation and measurements on this slice.

In the NLSY97, a person's answer about a given year, or at a given age, isn't always in one obvious round. This describes how NLS's data work and what NLS documents; which approach fits an analysis is the user's choice.

Why answers spread.

  • Rounds change frequency. Rounds 1–15 were annual (1997–2011), rounds 16–21 every two years (2013–2023). Fielding "began in the fall of the survey year and continued through the spring of the following year" (Interview Methods).
  • People miss rounds and come back. In this slice, 44% of respondents missed at least one round and were interviewed again, and 4.8% of pairs of consecutive interviews skip a round. A round in which a person wasn't interviewed has the code -5 (non-interview) in every variable, and RNI gives the reason.
  • Many questions ask about the time "since the date of last interview" (DLI). So the reference period is each person's own, from their previous interview to this one. After a missed round it covers the gap: NLS collects "detailed retrospective information about work history, education, training, marital status, and fertility since the date of the respondent's last interview" (Retention & Reasons for Non-Interview).
  • Wording and universes change by round. YSAQ-360C asks "since the last interview" through 2011 and "within the past twelve months" in 2013 and 2015. "Ever" questions (YSAQ-359, YSAQ-363) were asked of everyone in 1997, and later only of those who hadn't answered as of the last interview. In each record, questions[].waves and the universe by wave say which.

What NLS recommends.

  • "Researchers analyzing topics where time periods are critical should carefully examine the reference period of the questions and the actual interview date for individual respondents" (Interview Methods).
  • For the interview date, use CV_INTERVIEW_DATE~M and ~Y (rounds 2 on) or CV_INTERVIEW_CMONTH (continuous months, January 1980 = 1). For the date of the previous interview, find the round the respondent was last interviewed, then take that round's interview date (same page).
  • For status at a point in time, NLS builds event history arrays: employment by week, marital and cohabitation status by month, program participation, schooling, arrests and incarceration. "Using these arrays, researchers can extract the status of a respondent at a point in time or over time." They run from age 14 (12 for arrests) to the last interview (Codebook Supplement, Appendix 6).
  • Created variables (CV_ and CVC_ names) resolve common cases: the age at interview (CV_AGE_INT_DATE), "the round in which the respondent was last interviewed" (CVC_RND), and cumulative versions across rounds (CVC_, "regardless of interview status") (Created Variable Appendices; the CV_HGC_EVER_EDT codebook note).

In this repo.

  • person_year has one row per respondent and survey year, so a question's answers over time are one column.
  • CV_INTERVIEW_CMONTH and CV_AGE_INT_DATE give each row's interview month and age. MAR_STATUS_YYYY.MM, in person, is NLS's monthly marital array (group array-mar-status).
  • To find a person's answer about year Y or at age A, the options are:
    1. the round whose interview is at that age, from CV_AGE_INT_DATE. In this slice, 14–27% of people have no interview at a given age from 16 to 25, and about half at 30 and 35;
    2. the round or rounds whose reference period covers it, for a since-the-last-interview question: from the previous interview's CV_INTERVIEW_CMONTH to this one's. For YSAQ-360C, about half of people have two or more answers whose periods overlap a given year in 2005–2010, and with twelve-month questions in a two-year cycle, 80% of people have no answer whose period overlaps 2012;
    3. NLS's event history array, for the statuses it covers. In this slice, MAR_STATUS has a value for the month a person turned 25 for 94% of respondents, against 79% with at least one interview at age 25.
  • pdt diff . 1997-2023 --waves lists each record's changes between rounds: wording, universe, codes.

Finding the candidates with code: pdt.panel.

  • Panel(repo).answers(name, pubid, year=Y) or age=A returns every round's answer that could be the one about year Y or at age A. Each comes with:
    • its round, interview month and age;
    • its reference period, taken from the wording's reference_period;
    • how many months of Y it covers, or how far its age is from A;
    • the universe that round.

If there's none, it returns the reasons, such as "not interviewed (noninterview code 96)".

  • It never chooses. pick(candidates, policy) does, with a policy you name: exact, nearest, most_overlap or latest. It reports a tie between disagreeing answers instead of breaking it, and keeps every candidate.
  • dataset.yaml's panel.month_zero: "1979-12" places NLS's continuous months in the calendar: January 1980 is month 1 (Codebook Supplement, Appendix 7).
  • scripts/panel_check.py checks it against scripts/measure_spread.py: the counts agree for 2005, 2010 and 2012.
from pdt.panel import Panel, pick
p = Panel("~/pdt-nlsy97")
cands = p.answers("YSAQ-360C", 1, year=2005)      # 2005 round: 11 months of 2005; 2006 round: 1 month
pick(cands, "most_overlap").answer.wave          # 2005, because the policy says so
